“What nonsense,” Natasha suddenly said, “about the honeymoon and the first period being the happiest. On the contrary, now is the best time. If only you were not going away. Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And I was always to blame. Always me. And what we quarreled about—I do not even remember.”

“Always about the same thing,” said Pierre, smiling jeal—

“Do not say it, I cannot bear it,” Natasha cried. And a cold, angry gleam lit up her eyes. “Did you see her?” she added after a pause.

“No, and even if I had seen her, I would not have recognized her.”

They were silent.

“Oh, do you know? When you were speaking in the study, I was looking at you,” Natasha began, evidently trying to drive away the cloud that had come over her. “You are as like him as two drops of water, like the little boy. (That was what she called her son.) Oh, it is time I went to him... It has come... And I am sorry to leave.”

They were silent for several seconds. Then suddenly, at the very same moment, they turned toward each other and began to say something. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm; Natasha, with a quiet, happy smile. Having collided, they both stopped, each yielding the floor to the other.

“No, what were you going to say? Speak, speak.”

“No, you tell me; mine is just nonsense,” said Natasha.

Pierre said what he had begun to say. It was a continuation of his self-satisfied reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he had been called upon to give a new direction to all Russian society and to the whole world.

“I only wanted to say that all ideas that have enormous consequences are always simple. My whole idea is that if vicious people are united among themselves and constitute a force, then honest people need only do the same. It is so simple.”

“Yes.”

“And what did you want to say?”

“Oh, just nonsense.”

“No, tell me anyway.”

“It was nothing, a trifle,” said Natasha, her smile shining still more brightly. “I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today the nurse came up to take him from me, and he laughed, screwed up his eyes, and pressed himself against me—he must have thought he was hiding. Terribly sweet. There he is crying. Well, goodbye!” And she left the room.

At the same time, downstairs, in the part of the house occupied by little Nikolai Bolkonsky, the icon lamp was burning in his bedroom as usual (the boy was afraid of the dark, and they had been unable to cure him of this failing). Dessalles was asleep, propped high on his four pillows, and his Roman nose was emitting regular sounds of snoring. Little Nikolai, who had just awakened in a cold sweat, sat on his bed with his eyes wide open and stared straight ahead. A terrible dream had awakened him. In his dream he had seen himself and Pierre wearing helmets like those depicted in the edition of Plutarch. He and Uncle Pierre were marching at the head of an enormous army. This army consisted of white, slanting lines that filled the air like the strands of gossamer that fly about in autumn and that Dessalles called the Virgin’s thread. Ahead of them was glory, like those same threads, only somewhat denser. They—he and Pierre—were borne lightly and joyfully closer and closer to their goal. Suddenly the threads that moved them began to weaken and become entangled; it became difficult to go on. And Uncle Nikolai Ilyich stopped before them in a menacing and stern posture.

“Did you do this?” he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens. “I loved you, but Arakcheev ordered me to do it, and I shall kill the first person who moves forward.” Little Nikolai looked around at Pierre, but Pierre was no longer there. Pierre was his father—Prince Andrei—and his father had no image or form, but he was there, and on seeing him, little Nikolai felt a weakness born of love: he felt himself powerless, boneless, and fluid. His father caressed him and pitied him. But Uncle Nikolai Ilyich advanced closer and closer upon them. Terror seized little Nikolai, and he awoke.

“Father,” he thought. “Father (despite the fact that there were two similar portraits in the house, little Nikolai never imagined Prince Andrei in human form), Father was with me and caressed me. He approved of me; he approved of Uncle Pierre. Whatever Uncle Pierre says, I shall do it. Mucius Scaevola burned his hand. But why should the same thing not happen in my life too? I know they want me to study. And I will study. But someday I shall stop; and then I shall do it. I ask only one thing of God: that what happened to the men in Plutarch may happen to me, and I shall do the same. I shall do better. Everyone will know me, everyone will love me, everyone will admire me.” And suddenly little Nikolai felt sobs seize his chest, and he began to cry.

“Are you unwell?” Dessalles’s voice was heard.

“No,” little Nikolai replied, and lay down on his pillow. “He is kind and good; I love him,” he thought of Dessalles. “And Uncle Pierre! Oh, what a wonderful man! And Father? Father! Father! Yes, I shall do something that even he would be pleased with...”

PART TWO

I

The subject of history is the life of peoples and of humanity. To grasp directly and encompass in words—to describe—the life not merely of humanity, but even of a single people, appears impossible.

Earlier historians often employed one simple device in order to describe and grasp the seemingly elusive life of a people. They described the activity of individual men who ruled the people; and for them, that activity expressed the activity of the entire people.

To the questions of how individual men compelled peoples to act according to their will, and what governed the will of those men themselves, historians answered the first question by acknowledging the will of the Deity, which subjected peoples to the will of one chosen man, and the second question by acknowledging the same Deity, which directed the will of the chosen man toward its predestined goal.

Thus these questions were resolved through faith in the direct participation of the Deity in the affairs of humanity.

The new science of history has, in theory, rejected both of these propositions.

It would seem that, having rejected the beliefs of the ancients concerning the subordination of men to the Deity and the definite goal toward which peoples are led, the new science should have studied not the manifestations of power but the causes that produce it. But it has not done so. Having rejected in theory the views of earlier historians, it follows them in practice.

In place of men endowed with divine power and directly guided by the will of the Deity, modern history has put either heroes endowed with extraordinary, superhuman abilities, or simply men of the most varied qualities, from monarchs to journalists, who guide the masses. In place of the former goals of the Jewish, Greek, and Roman peoples—goals pleasing to the Deity—which to the ancients appeared to be the goals of humanity’s movement, modern history has put its own goals: the welfare of the French, German, and English peoples and, at its highest level of abstraction, the welfare of the civilization of all humanity, by which are usually meant the peoples occupying a small northwestern corner of a large continent.
